Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.

Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246]
and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by
TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security
(DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2
[RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further
deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.
Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status.¶
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:¶
They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.¶
There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites, especially
authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers,
which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2. Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in the
registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447], which indicates that such entries are not
recommended by the IETF.¶
The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.¶
The authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures.¶

verdict.summary:
# Answer

**1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (May 2021), which is part of BCP 195 (Best Current Practice) and whose memo status is "Internet Best Current Practice."

**2. RFC 8996 moved the RFCs that defined those versions to Historic status** — i.e. it reclassified them from Standards Track to **Historic**.

The two defining documents named explicitly in RFC 8996:

| TLS version | Defining RFC | Title | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 (January 1999) | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 (April 2006; obsoletes RFC 2246) | **Historic** |

So the short form of the answer is: **RFC 8996; status = Historie.**

## Evidence (verbatim, from the fetched RFC Editor pages)

RFC 8996, Abstract:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been **moved to Historic status**. … This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1. … This document also updates the best practices for TLS usage in RFC 7568; hence, it is part of BCP 195."

RFC 8996, body (Section 1/2):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC 2246] and 1.1 [RFC 4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC 5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC 8446]. … Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been **moved to Historic status**."

Corroboration on the receiving end — the RFC Editor index pages for the defining documents now show the reassigned status:

- RFC 2246 page: "RFC 2246: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 … **Historic** … This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 4346."
- RFC 4346 page: "RFC 4346: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 … **Historic** … This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 5246."

## Precision notes (things that are easy to get wrong)

1. **"Historic" is the answer to ask 2; "Obsolete" is not.** Both RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 had *already* been obsoleted long before — 2246 by 4346 (2006), and 4346 by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2, 2008). Obsolescence means "a newer specification supersedes this one"; Historic is the standarts-track disposition that says "this specification is no longer a candidate for the standards track and should not be used for new work." RFC 8996 is the document that performed the latter.
2. **Do not confuse RFC 8996's own status with the status it assigned.** RFC 8996 itself is an "Internet Best Current Practice" (BCP 195, updating RFC 7568). That is the status *of the deprecating memo*, not of the deprected protocol documents.
3. **Scope of the deprecation is broader than just TLS.** RFC 8996 also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) — explicitly *not* DTLS 1.2, and it notes there is no DTLS 1.1 — and it moves RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS) to Historic as a consequence. It also updates a long list of RFCs that normatively refer to TLS 1.0/1.1. None of that changes answers 1 and 2, but it should not be silently dropped in a compliance write-up.
4. **Nothing else deprecated these versions.** RFC 6176 (TLS 1.0/1.1 forbidding renegotiation), RFC 7567 (fallback SCSV), and RFC 7568 (BCP 195 best practices) all *restricted* TLS 1.0/1.1 usage but did not deprecate the protocol versions or reclassify the defining RFCs. RFC 8996 is the unique answer to ask 1.

## Citation block (ready to paste)

> Moriarty, K., Ed. and S. Farrell, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", BCP 195, RFC 8996, DOI 10.17487/RFC 8996, May 2021. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html> (Abstract; Sections 1–2).
>
> Dierks, T. and C. Allen, "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0", RFC 2246, DOI 10.17487/RFC 2246, January 1999. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2246> (status: Historie).
>
> Dierks, T. and E. Rescorla, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1", RFC 4346, DOI 10.17487/RFC 4346, April 2006. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4346> (status: Historie).

(Author lists and dates for RFC 8996 come from the RFC header block and were not part of the fetched excerpts; verify against the RFC's first page if the citation must be exact. The RFC numbers, the deprecation statement, and the Historic status assignment are all directly grounded in the fetched text.)

## Verification procedure (30 seconds, if you need to re-check)

1. Open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html>.
2. Read the Abstract: it names RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 and says they "have been moved to Historic status."
3. Read the header/"Status of This Memo": it says "Internet Best Current Practice" — confirming point 2 above.
4. Open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2246> and <…/rfc4346>; both index pages render "Historic" in the status slot. Done.

## One-line answer

**RFC 8996 (BCP 195) deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved their defining RFCs, RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1), to Historic status.**

Baltimore, MD – The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced today that Social Security benefits, including Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments for 75 million Americans will increase 2.8 percent in 2026. On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by about $56 per month starting in January.

quotes.whole:
Over the last decade the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) increase has averaged about 3.1 percent. The COLA was 2.5 percent in 2025.
Nearly 71 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 2.8 percent COLA beginning in January 2026. Increased payments to nearly 7.5 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2025. (Note: Some people receive both Social Security benefits and SSI).
"Social Security is a promise kept, and the annual cost-of-living adjustment is one way we are working to make sure benefits reflect today’s economic realities and continue to provide a foundation of security," said Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano. “The cost-of-living adjustment is a vital part of how Social Security delivers on its mission.”
Other adjustments that take effect in January of each year are based on the increase in average wages. Based on that increase, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax (taxable maximum) is slated to increase to $184,500 from $176,100.
Social Security begins notifying people about their new benefit amount by mail starting in early December 2025.

quotes.whole:
General
The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026. The OASDI contribution and benefit base serves as the maximum annual earnings on which OASDI taxes are paid. It is also the maximum annual earnings used in determining a person's OASDI benefits.
Computation
Section 230(b) of the Act provides the formula used to determine the OASDI contribution and benefit base. Under the formula, the base for 2026 is the larger of: (1) the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2024 to that for 1992; or (2) the current base ($176,100). If the resulting amount is not a multiple of $300, we round it to the nearest multiple of $300.
OASDI Contribution and Benefit Base Amount
Multiplying the 1994 OASDI contribution and benefit base ($60,600) by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2024 ($69,846.57 as determined above) to that for 1992 ($22,935.42) produces $184,548.71. We round this amount to $184,500. Because $184,500 exceeds the current base amount of $176,100, the OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for 2026.

quotes.whole:
Old-Law Contribution and Benefit Base
General
The old-law contribution and benefit base for 2026 is $137,100. This base would have been effective under the Act without the enactment of the 1977 amendments.
The old-law contribution and benefit base is used by:
(a) the Railroad Retirement program to determine certain tax liabilities and tier II benefits payable under that program to supplement the tier I payments that correspond to basic Social Security benefits,
(b) the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation to determine the maximum amount of pension guaranteed under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (section 230(d) of the Act),
(c) Social Security to determine a year of coverage in computing the special minimum benefit, as described earlier, and
(d) Social Security to compute benefits for people who are also eligible and receiving pensions based on employment not covered under section 210 of the Act. We credit a year of coverage, for this purpose only, for each year in which earnings equal or exceed 25 percent of the old-law base.

## Answer

**$184,500**

The contribution and benefit base (commonly the "taxable maximum") for calendar year 2026 is **$184,500** of earnings. This is the maximum amount of annual wages or self-employment income on which Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) payroll tax is levied, and it is simultaneously the maximum annual earnings counted in an OASDI benefit computation.

- Applies to remuneration **paid in 2026** and to self-employment income earned in **tax years beginning in 2026**.
- Prior year (2025): $176,100. Increase: $8,400, or 4.77%.
- This is the official, finally determined figure — not a projection. It was announced 24 October 2025 and codified in the Federal Register on 3 November 2025 (90 FR 49047, doc. 2025-19763).

## Authority and corroboration

Four independent official statements agree:

1. **SSA press release, 24 Oct 2025** (ssa.gov/news/en/press/releases/2025-10-24.html): "the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax (taxable maximum) is slated to increase to $184,500 from $176,100."
2. **SSA 2026 COLA Fact Sheet** (ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html), table "Maximum Taxable Earnings": Social Security (OASDI only) — 2025 $176,100; **2026 $184,500**. Same table: Medicare (HI only) — "No Limit."
3. **Federal Register, 3 Nov 2025, doc. 2025-19763** ("Automatic Increases to the Contribution and Benefit Base, Bend Points..."): "(1) The Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) contribution and benefit base will be **$184,500** for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026."
4. **SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base table** (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2026 = $184,500.

## Statutory derivation (section 230(b) of the Social Security Act)

The base for any year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y−2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only if a COLA becomes effective for December of the determination year; a 2.8% COLA applies for December 2025, so the formula is operative.

Inputs:
- 1994 base: $60,600
- 1992 national average wage index: $22,935.42
- 2024 national average wage index: $69,846.57

Computation:
1. Wage ratio: 69,846.57 ÷ 22,935.42 = 3.0453579...
2. 60,600 × 3.0453579 = **$184,548.71** (matches SSA's published intermediate figure exactly)
3. Round to nearest multiple of $300: 184,548.71 ÷ 300 = 615.1624 → 615 × 300 = **$184,500**
4. Floor test: $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-reduction rule does not apply and $184,500 is the base.

## What this means in tax terms (2026)

| Item | Rate | Base | Maximum OASDI tax |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employee | 6.2% | $184,500 | $11,439.00 |
| Employer (matching, per employee) | 6.2% | $184,500 | $11,439.00 |
| Self-employed (OASDI portion) | 12.4% | $184,500 | $22,878.00 |

- The base is **per worker, per year**, not per household. Each employer withholds and matches on that employer's own wages; there is no employer-side refund if an employee exceeds the cap across multiple employers.
- An employee who over-withholds because of multiple employers (or a mid-year employer change) recovers the excess as a credit on Form 1040 (Schedule 3, line 11) — the excess is not refunded by the employers.
- On Form W-2, this is the **Social Security wages** cap reported in Box 3 (Box 3 cannot exceed $184,500); Box 5 (Medicare wages) is uncapped.
- Elective deferrals to 401(k)/403(b)/457(b) plans **do not** reduce Social Security wages — they remain subject to OASDI up to the base. Cafeteria-plan (section 125) health premiums and qualifying commuter benefits *do* reduce OASDI wages.
- Self-employed individuals apply the same $184,500 base but deduct the employer-equivalent half of self-employment tax when computing income tax.

## Distinctions that are frequently confused with this figure (none of these is the answer)

- **Medicare (HI):** no taxable maximum in 2026. The 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer / 2.90% self-employed HI rates apply to all earnings.
- **Additional Medicare Tax:** 0.9% on earned income above $200,000 (single), $250,000 (MFJ), $125,000 (MFS). This is a surtax *threshold*, not a contribution base, and it is not indexed.
- **"Old-law" contribution and benefit base, 2026: $137,100.** Used only for Railroad Retirement tax/tier II, PBGC guarantee limits, special-minimum-benefit years of coverage, and certain non-covered-pension computations. It is *not* the payroll taxable maximum.
- **2027 base: $192,300** (computed from the 2025 wage index of $72,800.33). Wrong year — do not use for 2026.
- **Benefit-computation bend points for 2026:** $1,286 and $7,749 (PIA formula); maximum-family-benefit bend points $1,643 / $2,371 / $3,093. These are benefit formula parameters, not the contribution base.
- **Quarter of Coverage for 2026:** $1,890 of earnings.
- **COLA for 2026:** 2.8% (CPI-W, Q3 2024 → Q3 2025). The COLA drives benefits; the wage index drives the base. They are separate adjustments announced together.
- **Maximum Social Security benefit for a worker retiring at full retirement age in 2026:** $4,152/month. This is the "benefit" side of "contribution and benefit base" and is unrelated to the $184,500 earnings cap.

## One-line citable statement

> For 2026, the OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 — the maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll tax (6.2% each for employee and employer; 12.4% for the self-employed), per SSA's 24 October 2025 announcement, its 2026 COLA Fact Sheet, and the Federal Register notice of 3 November 2025 (2025-19763).

IR-2025-111, Nov. 13, 2025
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The IRS today also issued technical guidance regarding all cost‑of‑living adjustments affecting dollar limitations for pension plans and other retirement-related items for tax year 2026 in Notice 2025-67 PDF, posted today on IRS.gov.
Highlights of changes for 2026
The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000. The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over was amended under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0) to include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment is increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025.

For single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $81,000 and $91,000, up from between $79,000 and $89,000 for 2025.
For married couples filing jointly, if the spouse making the IRA contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $129,000 and $149,000, up from between $126,000 and $146,000 for 2025.
For an IRA contributor who is not covered by a workplace retirement plan and is married to someone who is covered, the phase-out range is increased to between $242,000 and $252,000, up from between $236,000 and $246,000 for 2025.
For a married individual filing a separate return who is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is not subject to an annual cost-of-living adjustment and remains between $0 and $10,000.
Other phase-out ranges and limitations
The notice also provides limitations for 2026 for Roth IRAs, the Saver’s Credit and SIMPLE retirement accounts.

The amount individuals can generally contribute to their SIMPLE retirement accounts is increased to $17,000, up from $16,500 for 2025. Pursuant to a change made in SECURE 2.0, individuals can contribute a higher amount to certain applicable SIMPLE retirement accounts. For 2026, this higher amount is increased to $18,100, up from $17,600 for 2025.
The catch-up contribution limit that generally applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in most SIMPLE plans is increased to $4,000, up from $3,500 for 2025. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a different catch-up limit applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in certain applicable SIMPLE plans, which remains $3,850. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 who participate in SIMPLE plans, which remains $5,250.
Details on these and other retirement-related cost-of-living adjustments for 2026 are in Notice 2025-67, available on IRS.gov.

The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. The elective deferral limit for SIMPLE plans is 100% of compensation or $17,000 in 2026, $16,500 in 2025, $16,000 in 2024, and $15,500 in 2023. Time for depositing elective deferrals
Employers must deposit employee contributions to the retirement plan's trust or individual accounts as soon as they can reasonably be segregated from the employer's general assets. The Department of Labor provides a 7-business-day safe harbor rule for employee contributions to plans with fewer than 100 participants.

Employer contributions
Employer matching contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make matching contributions for an employee who contributes elective deferrals (for example, 50 cents for each dollar deferred). Employer matching contributions can be discretionary (contributed in some years and not in others, depending on the company's decision) or mandatory, as in SIMPLE plans and Safe Harbor 401(k) plans.
Employer discretionary or non-elective contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make contributions other than matching contributions for participants. These contributions are made on behalf of all employees who are plan participants, including participants who choose not to contribute elective deferrals.
Types of employee contributions
Salary reduction/elective deferral contributions are pre-tax employee contributions that are a generally a percentage of the employee's compensation. Some plans permit the employee to contribute a specific dollar amount each pay period. 401(k), 403(b) or SIMPLE IRA plans may permit elective deferral contributions.

A SIMPLE IRA or a SIMPLE 401(k) plan may permit annual catch-up contributions up to $4,000 in 2026. Salary reduction contributions in a SIMPLE IRA plan are not treated as catch-up contributions until they exceed $17,000 in 2026.
Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees who turn 60, 61, 62 and 63 in a calendar year starting in 2025 and who participate in SIMPLE plans. For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $5,250 (instead of $4,000).
403(b) plan catch-up amounts
Employees with at least 15 years of service may be eligible to make additional contributions to a 403(b) plan in addition to the regular catch-up for participants who are age 50 or over. See the discussion of 403(b) contribution limits for details.
IRA catch-up amounts
You can make catch-up contributions to your traditional or Roth IRA up to $1,100 in 2026. Catch-up contributions to an IRA are due by the due date of your tax return (not including extensions).

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

2026 elective deferral limit (IRC §402(g)(1)), before any catch-up contribution: $24,500 per employee.

This is the officially announced figure, not a projection. The IRS released it in IR-2025-111 on November 13, 2025, and in the accompanying technical guidance, Notice 2025-67. It is an increase from $23,500 in 2025.

AUTHORITY

- Notice 2025-67: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025): "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
- IRS, Retirement topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
- IRS, 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, COLA increases for dollar limitations: 401(k)/403(b)/profit-sharing elective deferrals, 2026 = 24,500.

HOW THE LIMIT OPERATES (what HR should apply)

1. Base limit: $24,500 for calendar year 2026, for a 401(k) plan (traditional, safe harbor, or with designated Roth features — Roth and pre-tax deferrals share this one limit).
2. Floor: capped at 100% of the employee's compensation if compensation is below $24,500.
3. Aggregation: the limit is per individual, not per plan. An employee who participates in more than one 401(k), 403(b), or governmental 457 plan (or the TSP) must aggregate elective deferrals across all of them against the single $24,500 figure. Excess deferrals are includible in gross income and must be corrected.
4. Timing: the limit is keyed to the calendar year in which the deferrals are made, regardless of the plan's fiscal year.
5. Catch-up is additive and excluded from the question: age 50+ catch-up is $8,000 for 2026 (ages 60–63: $11,250), and is not counted against the $24,500.
6. Plan-level limits can be lower: the plan document may cap deferrals below $24,500, and ADP/ACP nondiscrimination testing (or the §401(k)(3) limit) may further restrict highly compensated employees. Those are plan limits layered on top of, never above, the statutory figure.

RELATED 2026 FIGURES (for context; none of these is the answer)

- Age 50+ catch-up, 401(k): $8,000
- Ages 60–63 catch-up, 401(k): $11,250
- Overall §415(c) annual additions limit (deferrals + employer contributions, excluding catch-up): $72,000
- §401(a)(17) compensation cap: $360,000
- SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferral limit (different plan type, not the 401(k) answer): $17,000

SCOPE NOTE

This is the federal statutory limit under IRC §402(g) for a standard 401(k) plan for tax year 2026. It is not a state limit and not a plan-specific cap. If the intent was the total including catch-up, or the SIMPLE 401(k) figure, or the §415(c) overall limit, those are the separate numbers listed above.

quotes.whole:
§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.



[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]

verdict.summary:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

ANSWER (primary, health-based standards, as codified at 40 CFR § 50.20):
  • Annual level: 9.0 µg/m³ — annual arithmetic mean concentration
  • 24-hour level: 35 µg/m³ — 24-hour average concentration (98th percentile form)

Both are expressed in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of PM2.5, defined in the regulation as particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. AUTHORITATIVE TEXT (operative section, 40 CFR § 50.20)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

§ 50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.

  "(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either: (1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or (2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.

   (b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3.

   (c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3."

  Source citation as printed: [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. STANDARD-BY-STANDARD TABLE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Averaging time | Level      | Form of the standard (how compliance is judged)                                             | Data handling  | Citation / rule           | Effective      |
|----------------|------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|---------------------------|----------------|
| Annual         | 9.0 µg/m³  | Annual arithmetic mean, 3-year average of annual arithmetic means, ≤ 9.0 µg/m³                | 40 CFR pt. 50, app. N | § 50.20(a),(b); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) | May 2024 (60 days after publication) |
| 24-hour        | 35 µg/m³   | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, 3-year average of annual 98th percentiles, ≤ 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR pt. 50, app. N | § 50.20(a),(c); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) | May 2024 (60 days after publication); level unchanged from the 2012 review (78 FR 3277) |

Reference/equivalent method basis for both: appendix L reference method or an equivalent method designated under 40 CFR part 53.

Rounding conventions used in the comparison (per appendix N): annual arithmetic means are rounded to the nearest 0.1 µg/m³ before comparison to 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour values are rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ before percentile computation and comparison to 35 µg/m³. A year of data is usable only if each calendar quarter meets the appendix N completeness requirement (nominally 75% data capture of scheduled sampling days), and the standard is evaluated on a 3-year average.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. RECONCILIATION OF THE 12.0 µg/m³ FIGURE — DO NOT REPORT IT AS CURRENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The source set contains two PM2.5 primary-standard sections, and they disagree on the annual level:

  • 40 CFR § 50.18 (text carrying [78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]): "...12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration..." — with § 50.18(b) and (c) phrased identically to § 50.20(b) and (c) but with 12.0 µg/m³.
  • 40 CFR § 50.20 (text carrying [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]): "...9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration..."

The 2025 edition table of contents for 40 CFR part 50 lists both "50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5" and "50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5," confirming that § 50.18 was left standing in the Code as the pre-2024 text while the 2024 reconsideration was codified in a new section. § 50.20 is the later codification (2024 vs. 2013) and is therefore the operative current primary standard; § 50.18 carries the superseded 12.0 µg/m³ annual level. Where the two conflict, the later rule controls.

Practical consequence: an analyst who reads only § 50.18 will report 12.0 µg/m³ and be wrong about the current standard. The 24-hour level is unaffected by this conflict — it is 35 µg/m³ under both sections and has been 35 µg/m³ since the 2012 review.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. CURRENCY VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how to confirm before publication/use)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Open eCFR, 40 CFR § 50.20 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.20) and confirm subsection (a) still reads 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, and confirm the source note is [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024] or later.
2. Cross-check EPA's official NAAQS table (epa.gov/criteria-air-pollutants/naaqs-table) — the PM2.5 row should show Annual 9 µg/m³ (annual mean, 3-yr average) and 24-Hour 35 µg/m³ (98th percentile, 3-yr average).
3. Search the Federal Register for any PM NAAQS action published after Mar. 6, 2024 (final rule revising the level, or a remand/vacatur affecting § 50.20). If one exists, re-derive both values from the newest final rule text.
4. Confirm § 50.18 is still the residual older text and has not been removed or amended in a way that changes which section is operative.

What would overturn this answer: a post-2024 final rule that revises the annual level away from 9.0 µg/m³ (up or down) or the 24-hour level away from 35 µg/m³; a court action vacating § 50.20 and reinstating § 50.18; or a change in the appendix N form that alters the numbers as stated. Absent one of those, 9.0 µg/m³ and 35 µg/m³ stand.

Note on the fetch date: the eCFR and Cornell pages in the source set were fetched 2026-11-17 and the § 50.18 text they returned is the 2013 text; the GovInfo CFR volumes reflect the 2022, 2024 and 2025 editions. The 2024/2025 editions are the most recent in the set and both reflect the 2024 rule, so 9.0/35 is the best-supported current answer. A live eCFR check of § 50.20 is still recommended at time of use, because the § 50.18 page returned by the fetcher is visibly not the whole current picture of part 50.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. SCOPE NOTES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

• Primary vs. secondary: the numbers above are the PRIMARY (public-health) standards, as the request specifies. Secondary (public-welfare) PM2.5 standards are codified separately (40 CFR § 50.7) and are not addressed here; the § 50.7 excerpt available in the source set appears to carry 1997-era text and should not be quoted as current without a live check.
• The request asks only for the two levels. Related items deliberately not answered here because they are separate determinations: area designation/attainment status under the 2024 annual standard, state implementation plan obligations, and the PM10, ozone, NO2, SO2, CO and Pb standards.
• Units convention: µg/m³ throughout; annual reported to one decimal (9.0), 24-hour reported as a whole number (35), matching the regulatory text exactly.

quotes.whole:
Toeboard means a low protective barrier that is designed to prevent materials, tools, and equipment from falling to a lower level, and protect employees from falling.
Travel restraint system means a combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection), and body support that an employer uses to eliminate the possibility of an employee going over the edge of a walking-working surface.
Tread means a horizontal member of a stair or stairway, but does not include landings or platforms.
Unprotected sides and edges mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
Walking-working surface means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
Warning line means a barrier erected to warn employees that they are approaching an unprotected side or edge, and which designates an area in which work may take place without the use of other means of fall protection.

ANSWER

In general industry (not construction), a US employer must protect an employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. The trigger height is 4 feet.

PRIMARY CITATION

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i):

  'Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

This is the current federal rule, in force since the Walking-Working Surfaces final rule (81 FR 82494) took effect on January 17, 2017.

DEFINITIONS THAT BOUND THE ANSWER (29 CFR 1910.21(b))

- Walking-working surface: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- Unprotected sides and edges: any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.

So the duty attaches when both conditions hold: (a) a walking-working surface, and (b) a side or edge of it that lacks a wall, guardrail, or stair rail, with a drop of 4 ft or more to the lower level. A wall, guardrail, or stair rail at the edge removes the edge from 'unprotected' and the 4-foot duty is satisfied by that barrier.

MEASUREMENT

'4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level' is measured from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level below. Exactly 4 ft is inside the duty ('4 feet or more'); 3 ft 11 in is outside it.

SCOPE AND EXCLUSIONS

1. Industry. This is the general-industry rule, 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D. Construction work governed by 29 CFR Part 1926 uses a different trigger — 6 feet (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)) — and is expressly out of scope here.
2. Superseded figure. The pre-2017 general-industry rule, former 29 CFR 1910.23(c)(1), used 5 feet. That figure is obsolete; any document still citing 5 ft for general industry is citing the pre-2017 standard. Answer 4 ft for current federal OSHA.
3. Jurisdiction. The 4-foot figure is the federal OSHA floor. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt a stricter (lower) threshold or additional requirements; the employer must check the State Plan standard that actually governs the workplace. (Oregon OSHA, for example, adopts 1910.28(b)(1)(i) at 4 ft verbatim, with state-specific additions.)
4. 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section.' The 4-foot general trigger yields to more specific provisions in 1910.28. None of those specific provisions sets a general height threshold below 4 ft for an unprotected edge; they either restate 4 ft for a particular surface or use distance-from-edge criteria for roofs. The employer must apply the specific provision where one exists.

SPECIFIC PROVISIONS THAT RESTATE OR MODIFY THE TRIGGER (for completeness; all consistent with the 4 ft general answer)

- Stairway landings, unprotected side or edge: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(11)(i)).
- Rope descent systems: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(12)(ii)).
- Slaughtering facility platforms, unprotected working side: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(14)(i)).
- Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(15)).
- Low-slope roofs: keyed to distance from the roof edge, not height above a lower level — within 6 ft of the edge, full fall protection (1910.28(b)(13)(i)); 6 ft to 15 ft from the edge, full protection or a designated area for infrequent and temporary work (b)(13)(ii); 15 ft or more from the edge, no fall protection required if the work is infrequent and temporary, plus an enforced work rule (b)(13)(iii).
- Fixed ladders: 1910.28(b)(9) imposes ladder safety system / personal fall arrest requirements keyed to ladder height and installation date, not to the 4 ft edge trigger.
- Holes, hoist areas, ramps, and other enumerated surfaces each carry their own 1910.28(b) provision; where an employee is exposed to a 4 ft or greater drop at an unprotected edge and no more specific provision applies, (b)(1)(i) or the catch-all (b)(15) governs.

WHAT SATISFIES THE DUTY

One or more of: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system), each meeting the criteria and practices in 29 CFR 1910.29. Where guardrail, net, or personal fall protection is demonstrably infeasible or creates a greater hazard on residential roofs, a written fall protection plan meeting 29 CFR 1926.502(k) plus training meeting 1926.503(a) and (c) is required (1910.28(b)(1)(ii)).

ASSOCIATED DUTIES TRIGGERED WITH THE HEIGHT THRESHOLD

Identifying and evaluating fall hazards; selecting and installing compliant systems (1910.29); training employees who use fall protection and who are exposed to fall hazards (1910.30); and re-training when workplace changes or employee performance shows the need.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A POLICY OR SIGN

'Employees on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, at an unprotected side or edge, must be protected from falling by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system.'

REFERENCES

- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (eCFR current; GovInfo CFR 2024 title 29 vol 5).
- 29 CFR 1910.21(b) (definitions of walking-working surface; unprotected sides and edges).
- 29 CFR 1910.29, 1910.30 (criteria/practices; training).
- 81 FR 82494 (Walking-Working Surfaces and Personal Fall Protection Systems final rule; effective January 17, 2017).
- 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) (construction, 6 ft — excluded by scope).

verdict.summary:
HELICOPTER VFR RESERVE FUEL — US REGULATORY MINIMUM

ANSWER
A helicopter must carry fuel for 20 minutes of flight, at normal cruising speed, beyond the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, before beginning a VFR flight in the United States. The 20-minute figure applies both day and night; there is no day/night split for rotorcraft. This is a time requirement, not a gallon requirement — the corresponding fuel quantity is 20 minutes times the helicopter's normal-cruise fuel consumption.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATION (Part 91, general operating rules)
14 CFR 91.151(b), verbatim: "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Note the contrast with 91.151(a) for airplanes — 30 minutes day, 45 minutes night. Those figures do not apply to rotorcraft. A helicopter flying at night under VFR still owes 20 minutes, not 45.

2. COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS (Part 135)
14 CFR 135.209(b), verbatim: "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
Same 20 minutes, expressed as fuel consumption rather than speed. So the answer is 20 minutes whether the flight is flown under Part 91 or Part 135.

3. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS AND IS NOT
- It is in addition to trip fuel to the first point of intended landing. It is not a portion of trip fuel and cannot be counted twice.
- It is computed at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption — i.e., use the cruise fuel flow from the flight manual or the operator's approved performance data at the planned cruise power setting, not climb, hover, or approach fuel flow.
- Wind and forecast weather must be considered in establishing the trip fuel to the first point of intended landing. A tailwind cannot be assumed for the reserve itself; the regulation states the reserve as time at normal cruising speed, so compute it at the normal-cruise burn for the type.
- It is a minimum, not a target. Operator policy, a Part 135 certificate holder's fuel policy, the aircraft flight manual, and prudent fuel planning for the actual conditions may require more. The regulation sets a floor only.
- No alternate-airport reserve is required for VFR; that is an IFR concept (91.167(a)(2)-(3), which for helicopters requires 30 minutes after the alternate, or after the destination when no alternate is required). Do not import the IFR 30-minute helicopter figure into a VFR plan.
- Fuel below the reserve must remain usable in flight — i.e., the reserve must be in usable fuel, not trapped or unusable quantity.

4. CONVERSION FROM TIME TO FUEL QUANTITY
Required reserve fuel (gal or lb) = (20 / 60) x normal-cruise fuel flow = 0.3333 x cruise fuel flow

Procedure:
Step 1. From the flight manual / operator performance data, take the fuel flow at the normal cruise power setting planned for the flight (gal/hr or lb/hr). Use the same units as the aircraft's usable-fuel indication.
Step 2. Multiply by 0.3333 (one third of an hour).
Step 3. Add that quantity to the trip fuel computed to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather.
Step 4. Compare total required fuel to usable fuel on board. If usable fuel on board is less than trip fuel plus reserve, the flight may not begin.
Step 5. Confirm the result also satisfies any higher operator, certificate, or flight-manual minimum.

Worked example (illustrative numbers only — substitute the actual type's data):
- Normal cruise fuel flow: 16 gal/hr
- Trip fuel to first point of intended landing, wind and forecast considered: 1.5 hr x 16 = 24 gal
- Reserve: 0.3333 x 16 = 5.3 gal (20 minutes)
- Minimum usable fuel at start: 24 + 5.3 = 29.3 gal
- Second illustration: at 12 gal/hr cruise, the reserve is 4.0 gal; at 30 gal/hr, it is 10.0 gal. The time is fixed at 20 minutes; only the quantity scales.

5. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Applying the airplane 30/45-minute day/night figures to a helicopter.
- Applying the IFR helicopter 30-minute figure (91.167(a)(3)) to a VFR flight.
- Computing the reserve at climb or hover fuel flow instead of normal cruise.
- Treating the 20 minutes as included in the trip fuel rather than additive.
- Planning to arrive at the first landing point with exactly the reserve and no margin for wind or weather change — the rule requires the fuel to exist at the start of the flight considering wind and forecast weather, and practical planning normally adds margin above the legal floor.

6. VERIFICATION NOTE
The quoted text is the current eCFR and GovInfo CFR text for 14 CFR 91.151 and 135.209. Fuel regulations are subject to amendment; confirm the current text of 91.151(b) (and 135.209(b) if operating commercially) at the time of use. The answer above — 20 minutes, day or night, additive to trip fuel, at normal cruising speed — is the regulatory minimum.

Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using

attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.¶

About TLS
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is a protocol that provides security for digital communications between two parties. When a server and client communicate, well-configured TLS ensures that no third party can eavesdrop or tamper with any message.
Supported versions
TLS 1.3 is the latest version of TLS. It was designed to be more secure than earlier versions and is the only version that will receive new features in future, such as support for PQC.
TLS 1.2 is still considered to provide strong protection against classical attacks when configured with the recommended cryptographic profiles. However, it will not receive new features apart from critical security updates, as outlined in RFC 9851.
If you use TLS 1.2, you should plan to transition to TLS 1.3 as part of your migration to PQC.
Deprecated protocols
The Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocol was the predecessor to TLS. All versions of SSL are deprecated and considered insecure. You must not use them.
TLS 1.1 and 1.0 have also been deprecated by the IETF, as outlined in RFC 8996, and should not be used.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**1. Deprecating RFC: RFC 8996** — "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021), part of BCP 195, status "Internet Best Current Practice".

**2. Status given to the defining RFCs: Historic.** RFC 8996 moved the documents that defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 to **Historic** status. Specifically:

| Protocol | Defining RFC | Title | Original category | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 (January 1999) | Standards Track | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.1 (April 2006) | Standards Track | Historic |

### Primary-source support

RFC 8996, Abstract (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Defining-RFC identification confirmed from the documents' own title blocks: RFC 2246 is "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0" (Dierks & Allen, January 1999) and RFC 4346 is "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1" (Dierks & Rescorla, April 2006), which itself carries "Obsoletes: 2246".

### Two status notions that must not be conflated

- **Historic** is the *status* (the maturity level in the RFC Editor / IANA metadata) that RFC 8996 assigns to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. This is the answer to the question as asked.
- **Obsolete / "Obsoleted by"** is a *relationship* recorded in the RFC index, not the status field. RFC 2246 was already obsoleted by RFC 4346 in 2006; RFC 8996 now obsoletes both. In the RFC Editor index, RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 therefore show both "Obsoleted by: RFC 8996" and "Status: Historic". If the requester's tooling reads the "Obsoletes" header rather than the status field, the answer is expressed as "RFC 8996 obsoletes RFC 2246 and RFC 4346"; either way the *status* conferred is Historic.

### Scope notes

- RFC 8996 also deprecates **DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347)** and moves it to Historic; it does **not** deprecate DTLS 1.2, and there is no DTLS 1.1.
- RFC 8996 additionally updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1 (and RFC 7525), and it moves RFC 5469 to Historic. Those are collateral updates, not the status of the defining RFCs.
- "Deprecated" here is an IETF standards-track statement, not a vendor or regulatory mandate. Bodies such as NCSC independently state that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 "have been deprecated by the IETF, as outlined in RFC 8996" — consistent, but secondary.

### One-line citation form

> TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) were formally deprecated by RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (BCP 195, March 2021), which moved both defining RFCs to Historic status.

OASDI Program
Earnings in Covered Employment, 1937–2025
People contribute to Social Security through payroll taxes or self-employment taxes, as required by the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) and the Self-Employment Contributions Act (SECA). The maximum taxable amount is updated annually on the basis of increases in the average wage. Of the 185 million workers with earnings in Social Security–covered employment in 2025, about 6% had earnings that equaled or exceeded the maximum amount subject to taxes, compared with 3% when the program began and a peak of 36% in 1965. About 83% of earnings in covered employment were taxable in 2025, compared with 92% in 1937.

is not reduced.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most wage/salary and self-employment earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is:

  $184,500

This is the official, final, announced figure for 2026 — not a projection. It was released by the Social Security Administration in the fall of 2025 together with the December 2025 cost-of-living adjustment (2.8%).

1. AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES (all ssa.gov, fetched 2026-11-17)

(a) SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, "Contribution and Benefit Base" — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html
The table "Contribution and benefit bases, 1937-2027" lists:
  2024  168,600
  2025  176,100
  2026  184,500
  2027  192,300
The page states the OASDI program "limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for a given year. The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used in a benefit computation. This limit changes each year with changes in the national average wage index. We call this annual limit the contribution and benefit base. This amount is also commonly referred to as the taxable maximum."

(b) SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 (specifications, dated 11/12/2026) — https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf
"The sum of this field and the Social Security Tips field should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026)."
"This amount should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026" (Social Security Tax Withheld field).

(c) SSA, Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026 — https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html
"Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026 (in dollars): OASDI 184,500; HI No limit."

(d) SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Detailed Calculator update page — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html
"Cost-of-living adjustment for December 2025: 2.8 percent / National average wage index for 2024: $69,846.57 / Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500 / 'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100."

(e) SSA, "Contribution and Benefit Base Determination" — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbbdet.html
Confirms the statutory mechanism and that 2026's base is the non-reduction floor for the 2027 determination: the 2027 base is "the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for 1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500," giving $60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, rounded to the nearest $300 = $192,300.

2. VERIFICATION ARITHMETIC (internal consistency of the stated figures)

- Employee OASDI tax at the maximum: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 — exactly the maximum annual Social Security tax SSA publishes for tax year 2026 in the EFW2 specifications. Consistent.
- Employer share: identical, 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00.
- Self-employed (SECA): 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00.
- The base is itself a ceiling, so no stated computed value can exceed a limit set elsewhere in this answer; the $11,439.00 and $22,878.00 figures are derived from, and cannot exceed, the $184,500 base.
- Year-over-year context: 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500 (+$8,400, +4.77%); 2027 (already announced) = $192,300. The 2027 figure must not be used for 2026.

3. SCOPE CLARIFICATIONS (avoiding the common conflations)

- OASDI vs. HI: $184,500 applies only to Social Security (OASDI). Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) has had no taxable maximum since 1993; SSA's 2026 Fast Facts table lists HI as "No limit." Medicare wages/tips reported on Form W-2 are therefore not capped at $184,500 (and must equal or exceed Social Security wages).
- "Old-law" base: $137,100 for 2026 — this is a separate computational construct used in benefit formula work and is not the payroll-tax cap. Do not substitute it.
- Rates: the 6.2% employee / 6.2% employer / 12.4% self-employed OASDI rates are statutory and unchanged for 2026; the additional 0.9% Medicare surtax above $200,000 (single) is unrelated to this base.
- Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to OASDI payroll tax for that year; the base is a single national annual amount with no state or regional variation.

4. CONDITIONS THAT WOULD CHANGE THIS ANSWER

Only a statutory change enacted after the fall-2025 automatic determination could alter the 2026 figure; none is reflected in any SSA publication cited. Before relying on the number in a downstream system (payroll, W-2/EFW2 reporting, benefit modeling), re-confirm against https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html and the SSA fact sheet for the year in question, since the base is re-determined every year and the page also carries the already-published 2027 value ($192,300).

IR-2025-111, Nov. 13, 2025
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The IRS today also issued technical guidance regarding all cost‑of‑living adjustments affecting dollar limitations for pension plans and other retirement-related items for tax year 2026 in Notice 2025-67 PDF, posted today on IRS.gov.
Highlights of changes for 2026
The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000. The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over was amended under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0) to include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment is increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025.

For participants who separated from service prior to January 1, 2027, Section 415(b)(1)(B) limits the annual benefit to 100 percent of the participant’s average compensation for their high three consecutive calendar years. Under Section 415(d)(1)(C), this compensation limitation is adjusted annually for cost-of-living increases. Notice 2026-66 applies the statutory formula to establish that:

This factor represents a 3.50 percent cost-of-living adjustment applicable to separated participants.

Notice 2026-66 increases the Section 415(c)(1)(A) ceiling from $72,000 to $75,000.

verdict.summary:
EMPLOYEE ELECTIVE DEFERRAL LIMIT — 401(k) PLAN, TAX YEAR 2026 (BEFORE CATCH-UP)

ANSWER
  $24,500
  The maximum an employee may elect to defer into a 401(k) plan for 2026 under IRC §402(g)(1), before any catch-up contribution. Up from $23,500 for 2025. Effective for taxable years beginning January 1, 2026.

AUTHORITY (three independent IRS artifacts, all agreeing)
  1. IRS Notice 2025-67 (the annual COLA notice for 2026), §402(g) paragraph: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
  2. IRS News Release IR-2025-111, dated November 13, 2025: "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
  3. IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
  Also confirmed at IRS Retirement Topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."

SCOPE AND APPLICATION RULES (state these wherever the number is published internally)
  a. What counts against the $24,500: pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals combined. They share one §402(g) limit; electing Roth does not create extra room.
  b. Aggregation: the limit is per person, not per plan. An employee must aggregate elective deferrals across all 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457(b) and TSP plans in which they participate. Excess deferrals must be corrected (distribution of excess plus attributable earnings by the applicable deadline).
  c. Compensation floor: the operative cap is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation. Low-pay, partial-year, and newly eligible employees can therefore have a lower effective cap.
  d. Plan-imposed limits: the plan document may set a lower deferral cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP) may force a lower cap on highly compensated employees. $24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not a promise of plan-level availability.
  e. Catch-up is excluded from this figure by design — see the table below. Do not add catch-up into the base limit when configuring payroll.
  f. Employer contributions (match, nonelective, forfeitures) do not count against §402(g); they count against §415(c) ($72,000 for 2026). Employee after-tax (non-Roth) contributions also do not count against §402(g).

2026 CROSS-REFERENCE TABLE (all 2026; keeps the base limit distinct from adjacent figures)
  §402(g) elective deferral limit, 401(k)/403(b)/gov. 457(b)/TSP ... $24,500  <-- THE ANSWER
  Age 50+ catch-up, same plans (additive, not included above) ..... $8,000
  Age 60-63 enhanced catch-up, same plans (in lieu of $8,000) ..... $11,250
  Maximum for an age 50-59 participant (24,500 + 8,000) ............ $32,500
  Maximum for an age 60-63 participant (24,500 + 11,250) ........... $35,750
  §415(c)(1)(A) annual additions cap (all sources) ................. $72,000
  §401(a)(17) compensation limit used for contributions ............ $360,000
  SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferral limit (different plan type) ....... $17,000
  SIMPLE catch-up age 50+ / age 60-63 ............................. $4,000 / $5,250
  Starter 401(k) deferral-only arrangement ........................ $6,000

VERIFICATION PERFORMED
  - $24,500 does not exceed the §415(c)(1)(A) annual-additions cap of $72,000 for the same year. Consistent.
  - $24,500 is the figure for tax year 2026 only. Notice 2026-66 sets the 2027 §402(g) limit at $25,500 (with a $8,500 age-50 catch-up). Do not use $25,500 for 2026; it appeared in the source set solely as the following-year figure.
  - $24,500 matches the §457(e)(15) limit for governmental 457(b) plans for 2026, which is correct and expected (the two have moved together), but they are separate limits applied to separate plan types.
  - SIMPLE 401(k) at $17,000 is not an alternative answer to this question; it applies only to SIMPLE 401(k) arrangements.

PAYROLL IMPLEMENTATION NOTE
  Set the annual pre-tax + Roth deferral election cap at $24,500 for 2026 (pro-rated per pay period as the plan provides). Do not suppress the cap for participants age 50+; instead allow the additional $8,000 (or $11,250 for those attaining 60-63 in 2026) as a separately coded catch-up bucket. Note the 2026 Roth catch-up requirement: participants whose prior-year FICA wages from the sponsor exceeded $150,000 must make catch-up contributions on a Roth basis if the plan offers Roth.

CAVEAT
  Figures are the federal statutory limits per IRS Notice 2025-67 and IR-2025-111. State or local rules do not alter them, but a plan's own document, collective bargaining agreement, or nondiscrimination testing may reduce the amount an individual may actually defer. Confirm against the plan document before communicating an individual's maximum.

The national primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for particulate matter are 15.0 micrograms per cubic meter
The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter
EPA is setting the level of the primary annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter

quotes.whole:
§ 50.13 National primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for particulate matter are 15.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration, and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L of this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The annual primary and secondary PM2.5 standards are met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 15.0 µg/m3.






(c) The 24-hour primary and secondary PM2.5 standards are met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.





(d) Until the effective date of the final Fine Particulate Matter National Ambient Air Quality Standards: State Implementation Plan Requirements rule to be codified at 40 CFR 51.1000 through 51.1016, the 1997 annual PM2.5 NAAQS set forth in this section will continue in effect, notwithstanding the promulgation of the 2012 primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS under § 50.18. The 1997 primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS set forth in this section will no longer apply upon the effective date of the final Fine Particulate Matter National Ambient Air Quality Standards: State Implementation Plan Requirements rule; except that for areas designated nonattainment for the 1997 annual PM2.5 NAAQS set forth in this section as of the effective date of the final Fine Particulate Matter National Ambient Air Quality Standards: State Implementation Plan Requirements rule, the requirements applicable to the 1997 primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS set forth in this section will apply until the effective date of an area's redesignation to attainment for the 1997 annual PM2.5 NAAQS pursuant to the requirements of section 107 of the Clean Air Act. The 1997 secondary annual PM2.5 NAAQS and the 1997 24-hour PM2.5 NAAQS shall remain in effect. The area designations and classifications with respect to the 1997 annual and 24-hour PM2.5 NAAQS remain codified in 40 CFR part 81 in order to provide information on where the 1997 primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS has been revoked and to facilitate the implementation of the 1997 secondary annual PM2.5 NAAQS and the 1997 24-hour PM2.5 NAAQS.



[71 FR 61224, Oct. 17, 2006, as amended at 81 FR 58149, Aug. 24, 2016]

§ 50.11 National primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for oxides of nitrogen (with nitrogen dioxide as the indicator).
(a) The level of the national primary annual ambient air quality standard for oxides of nitrogen is 53 parts per billion (ppb, which is 1 part in 1,000,000,000), annual average concentration, measured in the ambient air as nitrogen dioxide.
(b) The level of the national primary 1-hour ambient air quality standard for oxides of nitrogen is 100 ppb, 1-hour average concentration, measured in the ambient air as nitrogen dioxide.
(c) The level of the national secondary ambient air quality standard for nitrogen dioxide is 0.053 parts per million (100 micrograms per cubic meter), annual arithmetic mean concentration.
(d) The levels of the standards shall be measured by:
(1) A reference method based on appendix F to this part; or
(2) By a Federal equivalent method (FEM) designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.
(e) The annual primary standard is met when the annual average concentration in a calendar year is less than or equal to 53 ppb, as determined in accordance with appendix S of this part for the annual standard.

On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.

§ 50.13   National primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.

3) annual arithmetic mean concentration, and 35 µg/m
3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:

verdict.summary:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer

| Standard | Level | Form (how compliance is determined) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary annual PM2.5** (health-based) | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 consecutive years, less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20 (promulgated 89 FR 16202, Feb. 7, 2024; effective May 6, 2024) |
| **Primary 24-hour PM2.5** (health-based) | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 consecutive years, less than or equal to 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.13(c) (71 FR 61224, Oct. 17, 2006, as amended 81 FR 58149, Aug. 24, 2016); retained unchanged by the 2024 rule |

Units throughout: micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of PM2.5, measured in ambient air as particles with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm, by an FRM based on 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix L or an FEM designated under 40 CFR Part 53.

**Short form: annual = 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour = 35 µg/m³.**

## 2. Why these numbers and not the others in Part 50

Part 50 currently contains several PM2.5 sections because EPA has revised the standards repeatedly and left the older text in place for residual purposes. Reading the wrong section is the standard failure mode here, so the full map is given below.

| CFR section | What it is | Annual level | 24-hour level | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50.7 | 1997 PM2.5 NAAQS | 15.0 | 65 | **Superseded.** The 24-hour 65 µg/m³ was replaced in 2006; do not use. |
| 50.13 | 2006 24-hour NAAQS + retained 1997 annual/secondary text | 15.0 (1997 annual — not the current primary annual) | **35 (current primary and secondary 24-hour)** | Annual figure here is superseded for primary purposes per 50.13(d); 24-hour figure is operative. |
| 50.18 | 2012 primary annual NAAQS | 12.0 | — | **Superseded** by the 2024 reconsideration. |
| 50.20 | 2024 primary annual NAAQS | **9.0** | — | **Current primary annual standard.** |
| 50.13(a) (secondary clause) | Secondary annual (welfare-based) | 15.0 | 35 | Current but *secondary* — outside the scope of this request, listed only to explain the 15.0 that appears in 50.13. |

Two traps this table resolves explicitly:

1. **15.0 µg/m³ is not the current primary annual standard.** It is the 1997 annual value, now the *secondary* annual standard and, per 50.13(d), still applicable only to areas designated nonattainment for the 1997 primary annual NAAQS until redesignation to attainment. It does not describe the current primary annual standard.
2. **65 µg/m³ is revoked.** It is the 1997 24-hour level from 50.7 and must not be reported as current. The operative 24-hour level is 35 µg/m³.

## 3. Provenance and date of applicability

- **Annual:** EPA's PM NAAQS rule summary states: "On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS)... EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter." Codified at 40 CFR 50.20 ("National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5"), which appears in the Part 50 table of contents alongside 50.13 and 50.18.
- **24-hour:** Same EPA page: "EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards..." The unchanged 24-hour level is confirmed by the codified text of 40 CFR 50.13(a) and (c) (35 µg/m³, 98th percentile form), and identically by the 2024 print of 40 CFR Part 50.
- **As-of date:** the underlying sources were retrieved 2026-11-17; the codified levels as of that retrieval are 9.0 and 35 µg/m³.

## 4. Currency caveat and verification step

EPA's PM NAAQS page carries a March 12, 2025 announcement of a "path forward" / reconsideration of the PM2.5 NAAQS. No final rule changing the codified levels appears in the available record, so the operative standards remain **9.0 µg/m³ annual** and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour**. Before relying on this in a regulatory filing or a compliance deadline calculation, run this one check:

1. Open 40 CFR 50.20 and 40 CFR 50.13 on eCFR (ecfr.gov/current/title-40/part-50) and read the current numeric levels in subsections (a)–(c). If 50.20 still reads 9.0 and 50.13(c) still reads 35, this answer stands.
2. Check the Federal Register for any final rule titled "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter" published after Feb. 7, 2024. A final rule that revises the annual level supersedes the 9.0 figure in this answer; a rule that retains it does not.
3. Note that a change to a standard's *level* is distinct from a change to its *designations*; new nonattainment designations do not alter the numeric level.

## 5. Scope assumptions made (state these if you forward the answer)

- "Current" = the standards in force as of the source retrieval date (2026-11-17), i.e., the operative codified standards, not a pending proposal.
- "Level" = the numeric concentration limit. The form/statistical interpretation is supplied above because the annual and 24-hour standards are not comparable without it (an annual mean versus a 98th-percentile 24-hour value).
- Primary (health-based) standards only, as requested. The secondary annual standard (15.0 µg/m³) and secondary 24-hour standard (35 µg/m³) are noted only where needed to avoid version confusion.
- Units are µg/m³, the conventional and codified convention for PM2.5.
